This ECB version of the papal conclave brings its own cardinal challenges. Constrained programming problem: We describe this, formally, as a constrained programming problem with binary decision variables that determine whether a person is selected or not. It can be interpreted as a bipartite graph between roles and people (an assignment network), augmented by an institutional dependency graph that creates additional roles when certain assignments occur (replacement/vacancy propagation). It separates feasibility – captured as a system of logical constraints over appointments and the vacancies they may create – from selection within that range of feasible packages, captured by an explicit objective function. Feasibility: In addition to the standard bookkeeping rules – assigning only one candidate per role and prohibiting any individual from holding multiple positions – the feasibility constraints prevent any country from providing more than one board member, and bar France from providing consecutive presidents (not a formal constraint, but one we consider highly likely). Back to Back Hikes: In February the RBA became the first DM central bank to be forced to hike rates to control rising inflation risks. The expectation was that further tightening would be required. That said, a recurring debate with investors since that pivot linked to the quantum and timing of future hikes – with many suggesting a cautious approach to further hikes would be adopted. The energy supply shock linked to the Iranian conflict has presaged a more urgent approach to taming inflation risks with an unscheduled RBA communication that has triggered 70%+ market pricing for a back-to-back hike at this week''s meeting. The upshot for investors here should be that to control the inflation risks, the economy needs to slow, consumption needs to moderate, and unemployment will likely rise. This contractionary focus of monetary policy will likely be joined by fiscal in the upcoming Federal Budget. For equities, investors should focus on (for now) capped index returns, the de-rating risk that presents for banks, the margin risk that extends for consumer, the activity risk that builds for housing, and any further upside risk for the AUD and impact on translated earnings (more below). records.text: 6 Insights Information Classification: General Appendix Note on Percentiles We use percentiles to gauge the significance of a flow or positioning metric over a variety of time periods and countries. Th e percentiles have the advantage of making no assumptions about the shape of the distribution of the indicators, such as normality. Our use is aimed at being a simple way of ranking flow and positioning indicators relative to their own history. For all of the flow indicators within the Investment Climate, we calculate the percentiles based on the distribution of flows over the last five years using the daily aggregate time periods shown in the tables. Before calculating the percentiles, we constrain the 50 th percentile as equivalent to neutral. Flows above the 50 th percentile, therefore, are all positive and those below the 50th all represent selling of the market in question. A 100th percentile reading represents the strongest buying in five years; and a zero percentile equals the strongest selling. A reading in the 50th percentile would signal that net flows in the asset over the period are at zero. We use a simple colour coding scheme to highlight strong (top 20 th percentile) and weak (bottom 20th percentile) flows. We percentile our FX Holdings indicators in the same, conditional fashion, using the same five-year look-back period, as FX flows. records.text: 4 Singapore Economics - Pondering Implications of High Oil Prices While oil prices remain volatile, applying MAS’s Oct 2022 estimates that incorporate indirect spillovers significantly increases pass through from higher oil prices into core inflation. In a scenario where oil averages $80/bbl in 1Q26 and $100/bbl in 2Q26, falling to $65-70/bbl 2H26, core could potentially average near 2% in 2026 and 2027. Drags on growth would be felt via weaker external demand, but likely mitigated by lower oil intensity of economic activity. Should MAS see oil prices staying elevated, it would likely first respond to the clear and present upside risks to inflation, rather than to less easily quantifiable downside risks to growth, given MAS has been consistently tightening in the last 25 years when oil prices rose. While our base case remains for a 50bps slope steepening in Apr-26 for now (60-65% probability), should MAS see oil prices staying high for longer, more aggressive tightening options might be considered. records.text: March BoC Preview: Holding Steady At its January meeting, the BoC remained on hold, as widely expected, and maintained guidance that the policy rate “remains appropriate, conditional on the economy evolving broadly in line with the outlook we published today”. Since then, economic data have been soft overall. The Q4 GDP report came in broadly in line with the BoC’s expectations, but more recent spot activity data has surprised to the downside. The economy shed 109k jobs in January and February, and our CAI stands at just 0.1% (0.3% on a three-month average basis), although the unemployment rate edged down to 6.7% (vs. 6.8% ahead of the January meeting). On the inflation side, the BoC’s preferred measures also surprised to the downside: the average of the preferred measures slowed sharply to 1.2% on a three-month annualized basis (vs. 1.7% ahead of the January meeting). That said, much of the slowdown was driven by a steep decline in shelter inflation, which the BoC may discount when assessing the underlying trend. The most significant development for the economic outlook has been the rise in global oil prices due to the war in Iran. Applying our standard rules of thumb to our commodity team’s forecast upgrade implies a 0.6pp boost to headline inflation. We expect a smaller 0.1pp upgrade to core inflation. The market would still need to work through trapped cargoes, disrupted tanker positioning, elevated freight and insurance friction, refinery restarts, and the inventory holes already opening in both crude and products. In other words, reopening the Strait is not the same thing as repairing the supply chain. A large air pocket would still remain. "Reopening" scenario: In this scenario, the most extreme outcome is avoided, but the market would likely still stay tighter for longer than many assume. Barrels already trapped inside the Gulf would need to be moved, shipping schedules would need to be rebuilt, and refiners would still be dealing with delayed arrivals and disrupted product balances. Product markets such as jet fuel and naphtha would likely remain particularly tight even after some crude flow resumes. For that reason, we do not think Brent would simply fall back to its pre-crisis range if Hormuz reopens soon. Rather, prices would likely remain in a materially elevated range through 2Q and 3Q rather than reverting quickly to the pre-crisis ~$70/bbl zone, as inventories rebuild only gradually and logistics normalize only slowly.

records.text: tax dates. In theory, the Fed can limit or cap the total funds held in TGA. Historical precedent: TT&L program Pre-GFC, the Fed performed Treasury Tax & Loan (TT&L) operations on behalf of the Treasury. This allowed banks to retain tax receipts for a period to smooth TGA inflows and reserve outflows. It was effective in a scarce reserve regime when small changes in reserves had a significant impact on money markets. UST was also able to earn interest on these deposits vs zero at the TGA (deposits paid FF-25bps). In TT&L UST could also (1) make term investments (2) invest in UST repo. Post GFC, TT&L activity dropped & the Fed perceived it less necessary with abundant reserves (Exhibit 16, Exhibit 17). Modern day: capping TGA or TT&L reinstatement Capping TGA or starting a TT&L-type program is possible, but unlikely today. TGA cap or TT&L today would result in: (1) lower TGA (2) larger reserves in banking system. More reserves could then allow Fed QT restart & see Fed B/S reduction (Exhibit 18, Exhibit 19). The UST net interest impact would be a near wash since interest expense on debt outstanding would roughly offset deposit income. Drawbacks = (1) UST may not want a small TGA due to intraday payment timing considerations (2) banks may not want less stable UST deposits (3) debt limit episodes can create acute TT&L volatility. We are highly skeptical UST wants a smaller TGA. Foreign entities have tools to manage TGA equivalents TT&L type offerings exist abroad, including (1) B

Surveyed inflation expectations have moved higher so far this year, and tend to trace recent inflation. This is of course the feedback loop that a central bank worries about, though the question is the magnitude. Standard models of inflation (including the RBA’s) assume infla- tion is autocorrelated, i.e. has some persistence in lags, and that this represents households/ businesses forming expectations based partly on previous experience. The weighting on previous inflation is only partial, however, and as we showed here, this weight has been lower in recent years, indicating greater anchoring of expectations at the inflation target. This is also evident in falling unit labour costs, which have moved counter to the goods-driv- en inflation uptick since mid-25. Current levels of the MI survey are ~150bp lower than the 2022 episode, despite comparable levels of fuel prices. It is also worth noting that for this particular survey, responses have persistently over-estimated actual inflation by a large magnitude (survey average since 2016: 4.2%). records.text: it chooses the composition of its issuance, then changing the size of the Fed’s balance sheet should not have an impact on the debt available to the public and therefore on interest rates. The Treasury does not give formulaic rules for its debt issuance. But as the Treasury Borrowing Advisory Committee recommends, its strategy should consider the debt ultimately held by the public, or equivalently the liabilities on the consolidated government balance sheet that includes both the Fed and Treasury. This requires accounting for the impact of the maturity transformation performed by the Fed’s reserve management purchases (though not its QE purchases) and corresponding creation of reserves. If the Treasury does this, then shrinking the equilibrium size of the Fed’s balance sheet is not like QT because the Treasury should adapt its issuance in response—namely, it should issue more bills—which would offset the impact on the debt available to the public and therefore on interest rates.1 As a result, shrinking the Fed’s balance sheet would not tighten financial conditions and would therefore not create space for offsetting cuts to the funds rate. Third, even if the Fed could substantially shrink its balance sheet and the Treasury did not adapt its debt issuance in response, we are doubtful that lowering short-run interest rates at the expense of raising long-run rates would be popular with politicians or the public. Highlights this week We count 13 central bank rate meetings this week, offering an early read on how policymakers are weighing growth versus inflation risks from higher oil prices. For the Fed, we expect Powell to emphasise uncertainty, with the SEP largely unchanged aside from a likely upward revision to inflation. The Fed Board will also vote on Thursday on Basel III proposals covering reserve requirements for large banks and GSIB surcharges. Separately, Treasury Secretary Bessent and USTR Greer meet China’s Vice Premier He Lifeng on March 15–16. Most central banks are likely to remain in wait-and-see mode as the Middle East situation evolves, but the RBA looks set to hike 25bp this week. An unscheduled, hawkish interview by Deputy Governor Hauser just before the blackout period prompted us to bring our hike call forward from May to March. We also think the BoE will forgo a cut planned for this week's meeting: if energy prices stay near current levels, headline inflation could be around 1pp higher by July , arguing for caution. The broader point is that the loss of Middle East crude is already forcing refiners and end-users to adjust consumption. At the same time, the disruption is feeding back upstream. As storage fills and evacuation options narrow, producers in the Gulf are increasingly forced to shut in output, while refining capacity within the Middle East is itself being disrupted. Estimates from Rystad suggest that 8.3 mb/d of crude oil and condensate production is currently offline, alongside 2.1 mb/d of refining capacity in the region. That matters because once upstream shut-ins begin, this stops being only a shipping problem. It becomes a true loss of supply to the global market. records.text: Marvin Loh, Cayla Seder March 16, 2026 1 Insights Information Classification: General Classification: Complimentary Material March FOMC: Shocking developments The FOMC meeting this week will be shrouded in uncertainty, as there is very little clarity that the committee can offer on the war front. There are plenty of reasons to expect the meeting to sound dovish, including the focus on core (excluding food and energy) inflation and the potential for a growth shock if higher oil and a longer conflict emerge. At the same time, we think the hawks on the FOMC remain focused on its inflation target, which it has not reached for 5- years. From this perspective, we think the dots will remain unchanged, while the SEP will need to mark inflation higher this year. Powell may push back against interpreting higher oil only through an inflation lens, although the 1 -cut priced this year essentially matches the December dots forecast. This is also Powell’s penultimate meeting, so his views may be discounted unless it drastically pushes against current market pricing. Shock and awe: Prior to the start of the war, investors were generally comfortable waiting for new management to do the heavy lifting on the policy front. Any data driven hiccups were generally expressed further out the policy curve, and typically with a dovish lean. records.text: o we are watching for potential upside risks to inflation from this channel. As it is, the production cost structure for food is also linked to fuel (for powering farm equipment) and fertilizers, with the other costs being labour, seed and irrigation. Key inputs like fertilizer and fuel will eventually pass through. Moreover, as we highlighted before, in addition to the rise in costs, there will be supply constraints related to fertilizers considering the fact that the Middle East accounts for 22% of global fertilizer exports like urea, diammonium phosphate and ammonia. Who is more exposed? Within the region, EM Asia economies like the Philippines, Thailand, India and Indonesia will be more exposed to food price inflation risks (incidentally these are also the economies which are also exposed to fuel inflation risks). Given that central banks in these economies also target headline inflation, the potential rise in food inflation may be a concern to central banks and we highlight risks to the rate cuts we have in our base case for Indonesia and the Philippines. If the disruptions last for longer, we may get risks of rate hikes in India and the Philippines. In terms of output, India has the higher share of agriculture as 17% of GDP, followed by Indonesia at 13% and Thailand at 9%.

Layer two – suitability score: An ‘ideal’ candidate on paper may be politically infeasible, and the realities of political bargaining may favour a candidate with a lower raw similarity score. (Figure 5) We overlay our similarity score with these political factors through four channels. Adjustments can reflect 1) the number of senior posts already held by the candidate’s country in European institutions, 2) the country’s historical representation on the EB, 3) the assignment’s “complexity” measured by required position reshuffles, and 4) the need for a candidate to vacate a current role before term completion, which may affect perceived reliability (Figure 5). We also embed structural constraints at this point – i.e. a nation can hold only one seat on the EB at any one time. This assessment produces a penalty which is applied to the initial score to produce a final suitability score for each candidate for the relevant role. Differences in investor constraints help explain why IG, HY, and Loans can sometimes demonstrate varying trajectories on the same underlying signal. Balance sheet anchored markets like IG will have more price stability compared with flow-driven markets like HY that remain highly sensitive to sentiment, liquidity, and flows. HY’s strength and vulnerability HY has the most diverse investor base with 4 investors holding 25% each, shielding it from the vagaries of a singular dominant investor. This diversification is somewhat offset because ~50% sits in daily-liquidity vehicles, tying near-term spreads closely to flows and positioning. Pricing transparency and public-market liquidity mechanics nonetheless limit the risk dynamics seen in retail-heavy private credit. CLO dominance masks loan tail risk Similarly, within the Loan market, CLOs suppress day-to-day volatility through structurally mandated demand, but also lead to concentration of risk. This return profile of high dividend yields with limited underlying credit losses was very attractive to the US retail community, and US BDCs proliferated in growth. We estimate US BDCs now finance at least around $350-400bn of the roughly $1.3–$1.4tn private credit market (excluding dry powder). However, last year the BDC & private credit growth drive faced some unexpected potholes. BDC stocks last year fell 11%, largely on equity concerns. Fed cuts reduced BDC revenues given the floating rate nature of private credit loans, while new direct lending slowed as tighter spreads in syndicated markets ($HY bonds and $Leveraged Loans) offered more attractive funding alternatives. Rising concerns over potential BDC dividend cuts did unsettle some retail investors, although credit stress remained contained as Fed easing also reduced pressure on the historically high 9% share of private credit loans using PIK (“paid in kind”) interest to conserve cash flow. But in 2026, the fear from retail clients over dividend cuts has been compounded by a new concern, namely underlying default risk, with rapid AI adoption as the key catalyst. Our standard rules of thumb imply that our new energy price forecasts will lower global GDP by 0.3% and boost headline inflation by 0.5-0.6pp over the next year (with a smaller 0.1-0.2pp boost to core inflation). Following forecast changes in the US, Europe, Asia, LatAm, and CEEMEA, we now accordingly forecast 2.6% global growth (vs. 2.9% prior to the war) on an annual average basis and 2.9% headline inflation on a Q4/Q4 basis (vs. 2.3%). The recent selloff in front end rates—Exhibit 1 shows that end-2026 policy rate pricing has increased notably in the UK (+63bp), Euro Area (+50bp), US (+40bp), Canada (+39bp), and Australia (+31bp) since the start of the war—signals an expectation that global central banks will be especially sensitive to higher inflation given the recent memory of post-pandemic supply disruptions and associated surge in inflation. The size of the energy shock will likely prompt some caution, and we have accordingly delayed our forecast for cuts in several economies, including the US and UK. That said, the biggest policy risk from higher energy prices is that second-round inflation spillovers could lead to sustained upward pressure on underlying inflation, as occurred in 2021-2022. A key difference between 2021-2022 and today, however, is that today’s shock is more narrowly concentrated in the energy sector, whereas the energy price increases in 2022 were only one aspect of a much broader global supply chain crisis and inflation surge.

records.text: M Idea 6 The first acute dislocations are now showing up in refined products and regional shortages The first severe dislocations are now showing up in refined products rather than crude itself. That is not surprising. Crude markets are relatively fungible: one barrel can sometimes be replaced by another from a different region, even if only imperfectly and at higher cost. Product markets are much less forgiving. Missing jet fuel into Europe, naphtha into Asian crackers or bunker fuel in major ports is harder to replace quickly because these markets are tighter by location, specification and timing. In other words, even if some crude offsets emerge, the product side of the market can still remain acutely short. The clearest near-term pinch point is jet fuel in Europe. OECD Europe imported around 300 kb/d of jet fuel from the Middle East and China in 2025, accounting for roughly 37% of its seaborne jet imports. Following the Strait of Hormuz closure and China's announcement to half refined product exports, those flows have fallen sharply. The last jet cargo to leave the Middle East for Europe sailed on 2 March and the voyage to Rotterdam is typically around 19 days, which means the disruption reaches Europe with a lag. That lag is now beginning to run out. Unless Europe can attract replacement cargoes from other regions at significantly higher prices, jet availability is set to tighten sharply in the weeks ahead. Any changes to the Fed path could impact gold sentiment and ETF purchases: As seen in 2022, a geopolitical event that leads to rate hikes can be more challenging for gold, making the Fed trajectory from here important. Our US economics team still sees two 25bp Fed rate cuts this year, in June and September. Their rationale highlights that the Fed should largely ignore any oil-driven increase in inflation since higher prices tend to raise headline, but crucially not core, inflation. However, a sustained conflict in the Middle East could bring further energy price increases and heightened inflation risks – see The Oil Manual: Strait of Hormuz: Air Pocket. Persistently high prices may raise the risk that upward pressure on headline inflation is then reflected in core inflation, which could be harder for the Fed to overlook. Our US economists still note that "rising oil prices amid above-target inflation is more likely to make the Fed delay cuts – or cut more when it does – than it will move to rate hikes." For €HY, we expect spreads to widen from 310bps to 350bps by 1H’26 and then to 420bps by 2H’26. €IG demand technicals remain robust, but we bump our targets wider to account for weaker macro fundamentals than anticipated (pre-Iran) plus the view that higher energy prices for longer will keep ECB policy in restrictive territory for longer. Political risks in Europe are also likely to grow. n For £IG credit, we expect spreads to widen from 99bps to 115bps by 1H’26 and then to 125bps by 2H’26. The recent onslaught of issuance has exposed an important point. Unlike in Europe & the US, £IG spreads have been kept tight due to a shrinking market and limited net supply, not robust demand. The Cross-Border Equity Flow Indicator (xbEFI) measures the purchases and sales of equities by institutional investors, and is produced on a daily basis with a two day publication lag. The Cross -Border EFI focuses on trades by investors with base currencies that differ from a stock’s settlement currency. The indicator also includes transactions where the investor’s base currency is the same as the currency in which the trade is settled, and the settlement currency is different from that of the stock’s country of incorporation. An example of such a trade would be the purchase of a Dutch company’s American Depositary Receipts by a U.S. dollar-based fund. The Sovereign Bond Flow Indicator (SBFI) measures the purchases and sales of domestic and foreign sovereign bonds by institutional investors across countries and in regional aggregates and is available in unweighted and duration -weighted forms. We use unweighted flows in this document to capture the most relevant variable for a currency view. The SBFI is updated daily with a two-day publication lag. We use cross-border sovereign bond flows where available and total sovereign bond flows for all other countries.

However, it does not capture leadership styles, communication preferences or policy instincts, as those dimensions are inherently qualitative and difficult to quantify. The following points therefore reflect our own assessment of the channels through which different EB configurations could shape policy from 2027 onwards. We think, the ECB’s well-defined framework – anchored in strategy review, a symmetric inflation target and data- dependent, meeting-by-meeting guidance – will apply to any new Executive Board configuration. As such, no major policy shift should be expected regardless of the profiles selected. That said, individual personalities can still influence how policy is interpreted, communicated and operationalised at the margin. The allocation of portfolios across the EB also matters. Oversight of the Directorate General for Economics and Monetary Policy shapes the forecasting framework and analytical narrative; control of DG Market Operations sets the operational approach to liquidity. The president traditionally focuses on coordination and communication, but shifts in folder distribution can signal evolving priorities, e.g. around communication cohesion, balance- sheet philosophy, financial stability or structural themes such as climate integration. records.text: First, if the Middle East were a significant trade hub (that collected products and reallocated them to their destination), then a disruption in re-exports could lead to supply shortages. Exhibit 6 shows that trade rerouting could negatively affect re-exports of yachts and other boats, but the impact on other goods appears limited. Second, a reshuffling of global supply could lead to upward pressure on shipping prices. For ocean freight—which accounts for 90% of global shipping volume—this does not appear to be an issue thus far, as shipping prices ticked down last week according to the Baltic Dry Freight Index. In contrast, airfreight prices have increased significantly due to Middle Eastern air traffic disruptions, with cost increases to and from Asia and North America/Europe increasing by an average of 25%. That said, these spot price increases point to only 3bp upside to global inflation (with smaller impacts if costs normalize from current levels). records.text: iven by infrastructure investment. That said, the economy was clearly solid on track to hit the upper half of the growth target of 4.5-5% set by the NPC. Moreover, with upstream price hikes and recent oil shocks, we expect PPI inflation to turn positive as soon as March vs. our earlier expectation of June. This strengthens the case for the GDP deflator to exit its 11-quarter contraction in 26Q1E, providing a significant lift to nominal growth. The solid start reduces the urgency for imminent easing, affording policymakers space to focus on structural priorities. We believe the next few months are a critical window for delivery of the NPC policies. We now see a rate/RRR cut as more likely in 26Q2 or even later. Structural reforms, including tax reform and anti- involution, could be a near-term focus instead. The State Council has already announced plans to set up a “negative list” for local government subsidies aimed at curbing inefficient competition (Xinhua, Mar 13th). records.text: M Idea 2 Scenarios for Gold Gold has fallen 5% since the start of the Middle East conflict: After a volatile initial reaction to the start of the conflict, gold has come under modest pressure since then. In contrast, the USD has seen gains, with the DXY rising 2.8%, reaffirming its status as a safe haven asset. This is not unusual – gold can pull back initially during risk events: Looking at recent economic / geopolitical shocks, we observe that despite its safe haven status, gold can post short-term losses before recovering, as gold's liquidity can initially work against it as investors sell positions to cover margin calls or reallocate capital. Gold dropped 10% in the week after the WHO declared COVID-19 a global pandemic in 2020, and fell 5% the week after US Liberation day tariffs were announced in 2025. Both occasions saw gold rebound strongly over the six months that followed. The start of the Russia-Ukraine conflict also saw a pullback in the day that followed, although performance over the rest of the year was muted, coinciding with successive Fed rate hikes and a reduction in ETF holdings, despite an increase in central bank purchases. Arguably, gold's performance was much stronger than expected given the extent of rate hikes. Exhibit 2: Gold tends to suffer short-term losses before recovering during risk events. However, post the start of the Russia-Ukraine conflict, a rapid rate hiking cycle from the Fed held back prices. -15% -10% -5% 0% 5% 10% 15% 20% 25% 30% -20

records.text: lashing yellow, if not red We compare BofA (GFSI) and Bloomberg financial condition tightening in the context of 2025 tightening. BofA’s commodity-heavy GFSI is showing significant stress, comparable to stress observed in early April 2025, when the tariff-driven market meltdown that saw HY CDX widen from 350 bp to 476 bp in a matter of days was unfolding. Given the role of oil in today’s market, it perhaps is not surprising that GFSI is showing the most stress. Bloomberg’s index is at levels seen in late March, just before the April market meltdown occurred. We can’t say with certainty that further tightening in this index will trigger another meltdown. Simply put, based on last year, we see the BofA index possibly flashing red while the Bloomberg index is flashing yellow. The divergence between the two indices is noteworthy: complacency in some sectors? Stable SP credit index spreads: poor price discovery? We were surprised by the stability of ICE BofA ABS and CMBS index OAS this week, both widening just 1 bp, which contrasts with trading desk indications showing ABS spreads at least 5 bp wider across most sectors (and materially wider in aircraft ABS) and CMBS AA/A conduit paper around 10 bp wider. Palmer Square CLO data likewise showed AAA spreads unchanged and BBs tighter. records.text: opening of Gulf shipping; it was selective protection for Kuwaiti tankers, typically in convoys of fewer than a handful of tankers, escorted by 2- 3 US Navy vessels, and sailing only once every few days rather than continuously. Those numbers matter. If small convoys protected by multiple warships could only be mounted intermittently, then restoring anything close to normal two-way tanker traffic, roughly 70 transits per day, seen before the recent closure of Hormuz would require a vastly larger naval commitment. The practical constraints today are at least as serious. Convoys would need time to organize, escorts would tie up a meaningful number of warships, and narrow waters, mines, drones, missiles and fast-attack craft all remain real threats. Lloyd’s List argues that even in a best-case scenario, a convoy system would restore less than 10% of normal tanker traffic, with outbound movements likely prioritised first and inbound traffic only introduced gradually. On that basis, naval escorts may eventually help to move perhaps 2 mb/d in an optimistic case, but only after a delay and with significant operational risk.

Normally, this would lead to a bullish SGD outlook, with market participants adding long SGD positions ahead of MAS meetings. However, the current risk-off sentiment driven by Middle East conflicts has led to a strengthening USD, causing the SGDNEER to decline, as the USD holds a significant weight in the index (Figure 1). However, with the MAS meeting a month away, we believe this presents a buying opportunity for the SGD against the NEER basket. Historically, the MAS has responded to prolonged periods of high oil prices by re- centering the SGDNEER mid upwards, especially if it’s trading near the top of the band. This allows the SGD to appreciate sharply, mitigating the impact of higher oil prices to imported inflation (Figure 2). While typically a measure reserved for extreme circumstances, the current Middle East situation have started to evolve towards the tail risk scenario we’ve previously outlined, where oil prices surge towards $130/barrel (see Global macro: Crude reality (4), dated 4 March). As such, we think investors need to factor in the risk of a re-centering from the MAS, which adds to the bullish SGD view. Assuming a conservative marginal avg. cost per employee of ~$500k, potential restructuring could yield ~$7-8bn in annualized savings, which could reduce a portion of the $45bn in GAAP expense growth in our 2026 model. Based on cost commentary in the article, we do not expect Meta to materially lower its FY26 expense guide of $162-$169bn, though we view the report as suggesting cost discipline at Meta vs outlook. Bear case on the cuts would be that they are needed to ensure Meta’s outlook for operating income growth in 2026 in a more uncertain macro environment. Meta reportedly postpones Avocado release Separately, NYT reported that Meta has postponed the launch of its latest LLM, Avocado, to at least May, versus prior press reports that suggested a 1Q launch. The delay is reportedly due to performance issues, with the model underperforming relative to leading LLMs in areas like reasoning, coding, and writing. The report also noted that Meta has considered temporarily licensing Gemini models to support certain products while Avocado development continues. Our Take: Meta has indicated that the first version Avocado was expected to be “good” and not at the frontier, and the shift in the release timeline suggests Meta is prioritizing model quality over speed to market. Given MSL was formed in late 2Q/early 3Q’25, we think a 1Q launch timeline was ambitious and the revised timeline likely reflects a more measured development cycle.

We have been constructive on gold: We have been highlighting our 2H bull case of $5700/oz, driven by our expectations of continued central bank buying, Fed rate cuts supporting ETF inflows and a shift in investor interest in real assets. But recent events bring more two-way risks: While geopolitical risk can be supportive for gold, its performance in 2H 2022 (Exhibit 2 ) shows us that this is not always the case, especially if it drives inflation and Fed rate hikes. Our US economists still see two cuts this year, assuming the Fed is able to look through inflation, and we also note differences to 2022, when post-covid recovery also contributed to rate hikes. However, if the Fed does end up on hold for longer or even hiking, history suggests ETFs, which are often the swing gold buyer/seller, could liquidate some of their gold holdings. Our FX strategists also see two-way risks for the USD, which creates an uncertain outlook for gold. We also explore a stagflation scenario, which is usually positive for gold relative to other assets, while indications from the central bank of Poland last week that they would consider more "active management" of Poland's gold reserves raises questions about the future purchase path at the biggest central bank buyer. Our tracking for core PCE this year has increased substantially to ~2.8% Q4/Q4. Factors influencing our inflation assessment last week: (↔) January core PCE rose 0.36%MoM, closely in line with our 0.37% forecast but with some modest revisions higher to previous years and some surprising details. Core goods prices in January PCE were stronger than in CPI as expected due to the reweighting of various components. This dynamic should continue again in February (see below). Housing inflation continues to slow alongside shelter in CPI. Details of core non-housing services prices were more surprising. Relative to our forecasts, much softer prices for components like legal services were offset with stronger services like nonprofits and communication. Following the release, it became clear that a methodology change impacted the BEA’s calculation of legal services, with the source data switching from CPI legal services (which rose 11%MoM) to PPI legal services (which rose 2%). The change was not announced by the BEA ahead of time and details of the change are still somewhat unclear – for now we are assuming that PPI legal services will be used for this component going forward. records.text: Noel Dixon 17 March 2026 1 Insights Information Classification: General BoC : Staying on Hold Since the Bank of Canada's (BoC) most recent policy meeting, economic data has been, at best, mixed. The year-over-year headline inflation rate for February declined, primarily due to favourable base effects that are likely to reverse in the coming months. Through March, PriceStats MoM data has been trending upward, suggesting caution still may be warranted from the BoC. Concurrently, about a third of Canadian households are expected to see higher mortgage payments by year-end as they refinance, coinciding with a weaker labour market (unemployment rose to 6.7% in February ). Still, wage growth beat expectations while the participation rate has declined due to demographics and immigration limits. Should labour market conditions stabilize and improve, this development becomes a larger concern for the BoC to consider. Meanwhile, terms of trade have reached its highest level since October 2022, mainly from higher energy and commodity prices, helping counter recent weaknesses in trade-exposed sectors. Taken together, we expect the BoC to keep rates on hold at its 18 March meeting as it monitors economic and geopolitical developments. We expect the French presidential election cycle and the clustering of Executive Board mandates to sharpen the focus on that goal. European Council decides – leaders negotiate: Formally, ECB Executive Board members are appointed by the European Council acting by qualified majority voting, following Eurogroup discussions and non-binding opinions from the European Parliament and the ECB Governing Council. In practice, however, decisions are made in advance of this formal process. Political negotiations typically unfold over 2–6 months of consultations between leaders and coalition-building under QMV arithmetic, often embedded within a broader package of institutional appointments. Once consensus is reached, the formal process typically takes 2–3 months. The full sequence from initial political alignment to official appointment, generally spans 4–9 months. This implies that for mandates expiring in 2027, this process would need to begin by late 2026 or earlier, depending on President Lagarde’s intentions. Banks were net buyers of securities in the week to March 4 and in the wake of the conflict in Iran. records.text: March FOMC Preview: Greater Risk in Both Directions The most important developments since the last FOMC meeting are the start of the war in Iran and the spike in oil prices. For the Fed, the war increases both the risk that earlier rate cuts will eventually be needed to address labor market softening and the risk that a higher inflation path will delay cuts. But for now, the FOMC is set to leave the funds rate unchanged at 3.5-3.75% and will likely treat the greater uncertainty brought on by the war as a reason to remain in wait-and-see mode but ready to act. The Iran War and the US Economic Outlook We recently made several forecast changes to reflect the impact of higher oil prices and other effects of the war. We raised our December 2026 year-over-year headline PCE inflation forecast by 0.8pp to 2.9% and our core PCE forecast by 0.2pp to 2.4%. While we estimate that core inflation excluding tariff effects is now just 2.3%, we no longer expect any further progress this year because of the impact of energy cost passthrough. We also see upside risk to both headline and core inflation if oil flows through the Straight of Hormuz remain disrupted for longer and oil prices rise further (Exhibit 1). We also lowered our 2026 Q4/Q4 GDP growth forecast by 0.3pp to 2.2%. records.text: M Idea 2 Strait of Hormuz: Air pocket The disruption is now large enough to damage both supply chains and end-use consumption We are now two weeks into what is rapidly becoming the largest supply disruption in the history of the oil market. The recent closure of the Strait of Hormuz has disrupted ~20% of global oil supply, double the impact of the Suez crisis in 1956/57 which disrupted ~10% of global supply. By now, it is having a tangible impact both in supply chains and in end- use consumption. The clearest evidence remains the Strait of Hormuz itself. Our daily tracker continues to show a flow picture that is radically below normal. Since 2 March, just 0-2 vessels have been leaving the Middle East Gulf via the Strait on most days, versus around 35 vessels in a normal market. Of the 13 vessels that have passed through since that date, 6 originated from Iran itself, 2 were ballasting (i.e. empty) and one was a small coastal vessel carrying bitumen. At the time of writing, we count only 1 vessel carrying crude oil from origins other than Iran. In other words, the Strait remains functionally impaired. The situation has also worsened through the week in a more fundamental sense. Initially, crude continued to be loaded onto tankers that were already inside the Gulf, turning immediately into 'floating storage'. That temporary buffer now appears to be close to exhaustion. We also note that in 2022, it was not just the energy shock that drove rate hikes, instead combining with post pandemic government stimulus, surging demand for goods and tight labour markets. ETFs have been the biggest swing factor in gold demand in recent years, buying zero in 2024 and then 800 tonnes in 2025, nearly as much as central banks. With the breakdown in gold's historical relationship with US real rates, we look to gold ETF behaviour in rate cutting/hiking cycles as the swing gold buyer/seller (Exhibit 3 ). If rate cuts materialise, we would expect ETF holdings to continue to rise, albeit at a slower pace than 2025 given elevated price levels. On rate hikes or a more prolonged pause, we may see ETFs selling gold. This could also be meaningful if done in large quantities. For example, in 2013, ETFs sold 881 tonnes of gold, driven by rising US bond yields and fears of a 'taper tantrum' with the Fed indicating that bond purchases might slow (although this was not formally announced until December 2013). This undid 3 years of buying in 12 months. records.text: US Fixed Income Strategy | 16 March 2026 13 Agency MBS Jeana Curro BofAS jeana.curro@bofa.com Chris Flanagan BofAS christopher.flanagan@bofa.com Ge Chu, CFA BofAS ge.chu@bofa.com Ko-Hsiang Kao BofAS ko-hsiang.kao@bofa.com Commentary: beware the Ides of March March has traditionally been a particularly stormy month. Looking back at past Marches, recall Bear Sterns’ collapse in 2008, the European sovereign debt scare in 2011, the start of the COVID pandemic in 2020, Silicon Valley and Signature Bank blowups in 2023 and now the Iranian War in 2026. Before the closure of Hormuz, the Middle East Gulf was exporting roughly 1.2 mb/d of naphtha to destinations east of Suez. Those flows have now fallen to practically zero. The arithmetic set out above is already severe: even after allowing for bypass pipelines, strategic stock releases, naval escorts and some continued Iranian exports, the residual deficit still looks to be on the order of 10-11 mb/d. That is far too large to be solved by marginal offsets. It would instead require a meaningful reduction in consumption. The timing matters here. The shortage does not hit every region immediately because cargoes already on the water continue to arrive for a period. But if disruption persists for another one to two weeks or longer, the gap starts to propagate first into India and the rest of Asia, then into Europe, with the adjustment mechanism shifting from higher prices alone toward export restrictions, industrial curtailments, and explicit fuel-saving measures. In that scenario, the price response is unlikely to be gradual. Historically, real Brent prices appear to cluster around two broad regimes: a more normal range centred around roughly $75-80/bbl, and a much higher range around roughly $140-150/bbl associated with periods when demand is being actively destroyed. Any incremental Russian contribution is likely to come more through rerouting and sanctions relief than through a true step-change in physical output. Iran has remained one of the very few origins still sending some barrels through Hormuz, and for the purpose of stress-testing the balance it is reasonable to assume that around 1 mb/d continues to reach the market. That still leaves a very large hole. Starting from a disruption of roughly 20 mb/d, subtracting around 4.3 mb/d from the Saudi bypass, 0.6 mb/d from ADCOP, around 2 mb/ d from escorted convoys in an optimistic case, and perhaps 2 mb/d from strategic stock releases still leaves the market short by around 11 mb/d. That is more than three times the supply shock the market feared from Russia in 2022, and that fear alone was enough to drive Brent to around $130/bbl. The conclusion is straightforward: the available offsets are real, but but large deficits persist. That said, latest data also suggests China’s overall economic growth is unlikely to fall below 4.5% y/y in Q1, the lower band of China’s 4.5–5.0% growth target (see China NPC: Smaller stimulus for lower growth target, dated 5 March). From the perspective of our EPI framework, at these levels one should position tactically long, but given the noisy news flow, timing is unclear and caution is advised. However, their governing experience is noticeably less extensive than that of presidents. We omit Noyer from the centroid calculation because his career lacked a top leadership role before becoming ECB VP. Chief economists are researchers: The profiles of the four ECB chief economists differ sharply from those of presidents. Chief economists typically display strong academic credentials – as illustrated by Lane or Germany’s Otmar Issing – or extensive experience in research roles, as demonstrated by Germany’s Jürgen Stark and Belgium’s Peter Praet. All hold PhDs. Stark and Praet had long institutional tenure; Issing joined the Governing Council and Executive Board simultaneously as a founding member, having previously served on the Bundesbank’s Council. Lane stands as the only chief economist to arrive directly from a board of governors – as Governor of the Central Bank of Ireland. Indeed, we estimate that on average, global FX has moved by around 62% of its historical beta, with G10 currencies even less reactive – at 40% (see FX and energy Q&A: Strait answers , dated 12 March). We think the USD should keep rallying with energy prices holding at these levels, especially if – as we think is appropriate – front -end interest rate differentials widen out again in the USDs favour. This is not 2022 … but: Macroeconomic conditions are now fundamentally different from those seen during the 2022 energy shock, which means the central bank playbook will not necessarily be the same either . First, inflation was on a rising trend even before Russia invaded Ukraine; energy prices acted as an accelerator, not a catalyst. Now inflation is on a stable or declining trend in mo st regions. Second, there was a significant demand –supply imbalance that contributed to inflationary pressures, as the post -pandemic demand rebound ran faster than the economy’s ability to re -open fully. For example, the vacancies -to-unemployment ratio, often viewed by central banks as a good barometer of labour market slack, was at the highs. Now labour markets are tight, but not overheating .

US attacks on Kharg Island over the weekend, as well as Iran’s attack on the Fujairah port, are a case in point. What’s more, reports of mine-laying activity in the strait highlight that Iran can still disrupt the key global economic chokepoint even as ballistic missile capability is run down. And unlike economic warfare – namely tariffs – an end to airstrikes and other kinetic action in the Middle East depends on the actions of many players and cannot easily be ended or reversed through an Executive Order. The 2027 rotation will therefore determine not only who leads, but who controls the key institutional levers behind policy execution. Style issues: President Lagarde has consistently emphasised consensus-building, highlighted unanimity and explicitly noted the number of dissenting voices. Her approach prioritises cohesion and collective ownership of decisions, reinforcing institutional credibility during volatile periods. An alternative profile could tilt the balance towards a style where the president arrives with a clear view and uses the meeting primarily to refine and persuade rather than to canvass and synthesise. Both approaches may deliver the same policy outcome, but communication will matter at least as much as rates. A more proactive framing of risks could lower the bar for recalibration; a more consensus-driven style could lengthen deliberation cycles. Balance sheet philosophy: The ECB describes its approach as ‘quantitative normalisation’ (ECB, November 2025), with a calendar-based runoff and a gradual transition toward a more demand-driven reserves system. On the surface, the path appears orderly and predictable. In addition to weighting the ECB positions, we integrate the broader scope of all top European roles. A complete overview – including all prestige scores – is provided on pages 14 and 15. ▪ Reshuffle complexity: If an appointment triggers a vacancy at the EU level, the assignment becomes more complex because it demands additional political bargaining. The growth profile is also weaker, with recent revisions to GDP raising doubts about the economic strength at the start of the year. International conflict and oil—irrelevant at the turn of the year— have displaced traditional macro drivers such as US growth and, in particular, the labour market. This shift is evident not only in media correlations captured in our narrative map (Figure 3), but also in the dollar’s reaction to data. As we noted in Risky Revelations, the DXY barely reacted to a surprisingly weak February payrolls print, and the correlation between US data surprises and the dollar has fallen to a six-month low. What matters more in the immediate aftermath of shocks is positioning. One of the few narratives that has remained important throughout is crowded trades. Earlier in the year, stronger growth offered a catalyst for reassessing a significant DXY underweight; today, it is risk aversion that is driving a move back toward benchmark. Only once positioning normalises will it become clear whether the dollar has genuinely reasserted its safe-haven status, or whether recent strength reflects little more than a position unwind. That distinction will ultimately hinge on relative central bank responses to the coming inflation shock. As Figure 4 shows, central bank rhetoric remains widely dispersed, though it has become noticeably less dovish in recent weeks. records.text: Noel Dixon 16 March 2026 1 Insights Information Classification: General RBA Preview: Forced to deliver another hike Before the military conflict in the Middle East erupted, inflation was already a problem for the Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA). January headline and trimmed mean inflation both came in above consensus forecast s. Since June 2025, non-tradable inflation (which tracks goods and services affected by domestic demand) has been on a steady rise. Tradable inflation, representing the impact of international factors on prices, is expected to climb as well, driven by anticipated increases in automotive fuel costs. Together, these trends could push the annual headline CPI toward 4%yoy over the next few months. Meanwhile, Australia’s labour market is still very tight at 4.1% – the lowest unemployment rate since May last year and significantly below its 20-year average of 5.1%. Collectively, this will likely compel the RBA to deliver a second consecutive hike at its 17 March meeting. However, we believe rate markets are fully priced with 60bps of hikes expected by the end of this year. Real money investor positioning in AUD is exceptionally overweight, which urges caution despite our positive outlook on Australia's economy. Therefore, we remain short-term negative on AUD until positioning adjusts. Australia's CPI increased by 3.8% in January, unchanged from December. Travel tour prices fell 3.1% year over year, while cellular services prices rose 1.5%, slowing sharply from 4.9% in January. Going into March and April, we expect energy prices to substantially raise headline inflation, even after accounting for the remaining GST/HST passthrough in March. Core inflation, as well as Trim and Median measures should remain incrementally disinflationary, but not enough to offset energy effects.

BofA’s commodity-heavy GFSI is showing significant stress, comparable to stress observed in early April 2025, when the tariff-driven market meltdown that saw HY CDX widen from 350 bp to 476 bp in a matter of days was unfolding. Given the role of oil in today’s market, it perhaps is not surprising that GFSI is showing the most stress. Bloomberg’s index is at levels seen in late March, just before the April market meltdown occurred. We can’t say with certainty that further tightening in this index will trigger another meltdown. Simply put, based on last year, we see the BofA index possibly flashing red while the Bloomberg index is flashing yellow. The divergence between the two indices is noteworthy, perhaps indicative of complacency in some sectors.

records.text: E M – L O C A L E YE S FO R A G L O B A L V IE W A quantitative look at ECB roles: Multidimensional scaling lets us project the profile data of former EB members, including ECB presidents, into two dimensions (Figure 7). Aggregating so many variables creates abstract dimensions that are difficult to interpret directly. However, we observe that the two-dimension scaling results in higher x-values aligning with stronger academic backgrounds, while lower x-values characterise more politically oriented profiles. Higher y-values show extensive top-level experience in institutions, whereas lower y-values reflect careers concentrated on board-member roles. Despite the limited number of observations, we calculate Gaussian centroids for each role. We interpret these clusters as the typical profile for each EB role. Lagarde’s distinct background: Even with a small cohort of predecessors as ECB president, President Lagarde’s profile is atypical. Wim Duisenberg, Jean- Claude Trichet, and Draghi were career economists who had previously led their national central banks, held doctorates and (for Duisenberg and Draghi at least) occupied professorial positions. This creates a tight cluster of similar profiles in the data to which President Lagarde presented a sharp contrast. She entered public service after 23 years in the private sector and held top leadership roles in French government and as head of the IMF. As with the previous month, housing costs contributed most to annual inflation, followed by food, non-alcoholic beverages, and recreation expenses. A significant rise in electricity costs (up 32%yoy within the housing category) was the main driver. Through March, PriceStats indicates that inflation is being pushed higher primarily by increasing costs of household goods and food. The data has not yet reflected the recent surge in automotive fuel prices, which are part of the transport component of CPI. As a result, there is a possibility that headline CPI could reach 4%yoy in upcoming releases. Meanwhile, the labour market remains tight with unemployment at 4.1%, the lowest since May last year. This tightness is largely due to a lower participation rate, indicating a smaller labour pool available to employers. Given these factors, it is likely that the RBA will deliver a second consecutive rate hike at its 17 March meeting. Given the ongoing decline in the participation rate due to demographic changes and immigration constraints, the BoC will need to closely observe any material recovery in the labour market. Taken together, it is likely that the BoC will opt to maintain its policy rate at the upcoming 18 March meeting, as it continues to evaluate new data releases and geopolitical developments. From a positioning perspective, real money investors are roughly neutral the CAD ahead of this meeting. Notably, Canadian domestic investors have begun to hedge their overseas asset exposures (Figure 4). At the same time, foreign investors in Canada continue to decrease their hedges. This evolving hedging environment is supportive for the Canadian dollar in the near term. On a medium-term horizon, we retain a constructive outlook on the CAD, particularly when positioned against a short EUR. The underlying export-import dynamics (where Canada benefits from elevated energy prices while Europe faces negative impacts) support expressing this view via a short EURCAD position. But price increases may also reflect factors like higher costs for memory/storage and upward pressure on prices for computer products broadly (even for consumers) due to AI-investment demand. Previous price declines in this component could partly be a consequence of the quality-adjustment made to CPI prices, reflecting improved quality of technology and related products over the years. This could continue to be an offsetting force against higher costs. But further upside risks to this component are substantial if shortages and stronger AI-demand are the cause of recent increases. For now, we’ve upgraded our base case for computer software and accessories to include stronger increases over the next 2 months. This reflects the potential new seasonal pattern of the last few years, which has implied prices peaking around April/May before falling again. records.text: We also don’t anticipate changes in the 2027 and 2028 medians. They are currently at 3.125%, indicating that’s where the Fed sees the trough of the cutting cycle. We concur, somewhat grudgingly. We don’t think the Fed needs to cut any further, but the majority of the committee is still holding on to a low neutral rate view. This opens the door for additional cuts if there is any blip in the data, particularly since incoming Chair Warsh has been strongly advocating for cuts. We do anticipate a 12.5bp uptick in the longer-run rate, to 3.125%. This change is more likely if the longer-run growth estimate also moves up. Either way, though, it’s unlikely to affect this year’s policy path. Presser: renewed tension between the two mandates The March press conference will be Chair Powell’s second-to-last (assuming Warsh is confirmed in time for the June meeting). With an April cut almost entirely priced out, Powell’s ability to guide markets depends on the extent to which they perceive his comments as representing the committee’s consensus rather than his own views. Even setting this constraint aside, Powell will have his work cut out for him. Just as the Fed was starting to see diminishing tension between its two mandates, the spike in oil prices has created fresh stagflationary risks. Powell is likely to emphasize that the Fed is in “wait and see” mode. He might note that long-term breakeven inflation has been stable. But year-end Fed pricing has moved from 60bp of cuts at the end

Monetary Policy Response Will Not Be One-Size Fits All UBS Economists have discussed recent risks and see three policy pathways: (1) CBs who were planning to tighten for growth reasons may act earlier - MAS stands out; odds of a larger-than-baseline 0.5% p.a. slope adjustment in mid-April have risen. (2) if oil averages >$80/bbl for longer, CPI-near-target economies might deliver calibrated tightening in 2H (e.g. KR, MY, TW, PH); Not our baseline though. (3) Economies in easing mode could pause/end rates cuts (CN, IN, TH, ID). Rate Hike Expectations Screen Stretched; Where is the Value re-emerging? Recentering risk: Historically, the MAS has responded to prolonged periods of high inflation, caused by high oil prices in 2011 and 2022, by re-centering the SGDNEER mid-point upwards. This allows scope for the SGD to appreciate quickly, mitigating the impact of high inflation (Figure 2). While re-centering the policy band is typically a measure MAS reserves for extreme circumstances, given the current sharp increase in oil prices, we believe MAS may consider re-centering the band upwards. This measure would provide a faster means of reducing imported inflation compared to adjusting the SGDNEER slope. We think the market is underestimating the likelihood of a re- centering from MAS and therefore recommend running long SGDNEER. If oil prices were to remain high, exacerbating growth concerns, we expect the government to respond with fiscal measures to support the economy, allowing monetary policy to focus on maintaining price stability. The current risk-off sentiment driven by the Middle East conflict has led to broad USD strength, which saw the SGDNEER initially decline, as the USD holds a significant weight in the index. We estimate that countries in our coverage import more than USD 12bn of fertilizers from the region, accounting for over 16% of global trade—and more than 25% for certain nitrogenous products. Emerging markets are generally most exposed to these shortages. India, Brazil, Turkey, and South Africa are among the largest importers of Middle Eastern aluminum, petrochemicals/plastics and fertilizer. But risks extend further: Australia imports significant fertilizer volumes from the region, while Japan, Korea, Italy, and the United States each source at least 10% of their aluminum from the Middle East. Supply chains will need to adjust quickly, but the disruption is meaningful. And with Asia ex China manufacturing PMIs near recent highs and Euro area PMIs in expansion, the risk skew is clear.

Through late January, gold was running a rolling 6m correlation of ~90% with the S&P500 and 93% with copper, implying a stronger correlation with risk assets, rather than acting as a diversifier. In the last two months, the rolling copper correlation has held, but the S&P correlation has weakened, suggesting gold's "real asset" characteristics are coming back into play. However, gold's strength over the past 12 months also seems to be working against it, with weakness during the ongoing Middle East conflict rather than strength. The challenge with the current conflict is that it also brings risks of slower Fed cuts or even hikes, creating a more uncertain outlook for gold. MS Outlook: We continue to highlight our bull case of $5700/oz for gold into 2H but acknowledge the outlook is becoming more uncertain. If the Fed is able to look through rising oil prices and we see a more short-term disruption, driving rate cuts and a return to USD weakness, we could see further support for gold supported by ETF and central bank buying. The recent stability in prices may also drive engagement from potential buyers who did not want to chase the price higher. A more prolonged conflict and stagflation scenario could also be supportive for gold relative to other asset classes. However, if the shipping disruptions continue and market consensus starts to price in rate hikes on inflation concerns, then the set-up for gold could be more challenging in the short term

According to our framework, the basket is oversold by 3.1 z-scores (4.9% from fair value). After an initial move higher, its MarFA fair value has drifted sideways, suggesting that the downside move in spot may be limited. We are initiating a long BNPP US Quality (BNPUTLTQ) versus S&P 500 trade idea. The pair screens as oversold by 3.0 z-scores (8% from FV), according to MarFA Macro. Its fair value is mostly driven by MarFA Macro’s first principal component (PC1; 53%). As we flagged in last week’s QTOW, dated 9 March, the recent risk-off mood in equity markets has been accompanied by a decoupling of PC1 from earnings expectations. We think that a continuation of the conflict in the Middle East could result in earnings expectations being revised lower. If that is the case, positioning in higher-quality names versus the broader market looks attractive. A weekly close above 4.90%—the top of the triangle— would support a move toward the cycle highs at 5.15–5.18% and alternate wave (5) targets of 5.40% and 5.65%. This view holds while yields maintain higher lows (recently 4.60% and 4.52%). A break to lower lows would instead revive the cyclical bull trend toward, and potentially below, 4.00%. A top in the daily chart should also be monitored, as it could signal a near‑term decline in yields. Chart 1: US 30Y yield in a triangle pattern between converging lines now at 4.60-4.90%. In the case of a swift resolution of the conflict, we expect markets to retrace back to previous cen- tral bank pricing, implying a bull steepening from current levels (1Yx1Y ESTR returning to 2.05% and 1Yx1Y SONIA back into easing territory at 3.40%). Under a sticky resolution scenario, we expect markets to move back to pricing a more modest tightening than what is currently priced (1Yx1Y ESTR returning to 2.05% and 1Yx1Y SONIA back into easing territory at 3.40%). Finally, in case of prolonged conflict, we see EUR and GBP markets pricing in a more aggressive front-loaded tightening with a more marked bear flattening in the Euro area (1Yx1Y ESTR at 2.65% and 10Y Bund at 3%) than in the UK (1Yx1Y SONIA at 4.15% and 10Y gilts at 4.70%). Sources: Bloomberg, Macrobond, BNP Paribas Fig. 1: : S$NEER vs Input Prices We favour adding long SGDNEER exposure ahead of the Monetary Authority of Singapore’s meeting in April, via a proxy NEER basket optimised for accessibility and carry. Risks for hawkish MAS shift: Singapore’s growth has remained robust, while inflation has bottomed out from 2025 lows. Since January, we have flagged a risk of the MAS reducing its policy accommodativeness this year, as Singapore goes through a reflationary phase (see Singapore: Reflation set to change MAS and market views, dated 7 January). Historically, the MAS has usually done this by increasing the SGDNEER slope (Figure 1), which we estimate has a long-term average of 1.0% and is currently at 0.50%. The recent Middle East conflict has added to inflation concerns, given Singapore's reliance on oil imports and limited reserves (FX: Asia's sensitivity to supply-driven energy shocks, 10 March), increasing the likelihood of a hawkish move from the MAS in April. We expect the BoE will likely remove the previous clear easing bias (“Bank Rate is likely to be reduced further”) from the statement to lower expectations for near-term rate cuts, though it will not want to drop its easing bias altogether. Turning to the Euro area, we broadly expect a moderate ECB response to the recent energy price shock. We think that unless spot energy prices rise significantly above current levels and remain elevated for several months, the ECB will likely remain on hold rather than shifting to hiking. While the central bank will likely sound more nervous about headline inflation moving back above target, we think that this will be weighed against risks to growth and the risk of second-round effects that appear much smaller now than during the 2022 energy shock. records.text: M Idea 4 Two-way risks for the USD bring an uncertain outlook for gold: Gold and the USD can move together or in opposite directions, depending on the underlying economic backdrop. For example, gold and the USD can rally simultaneously if they are both acting as safe havens. In 2025 though, US tariff concerns weighed on the USD while supporting gold. Our FX strategists maintain a neutral outlook on the USD to reflect risks in both directions – further escalation could see further USD strength, while de-escalation could see the USD reverse much of its gains, with gold potentially a beneficiary in either scenario. Stagflation fears would be a positive for gold: With oil trading ~$100/bbl, concerns about global growth and stagflation are rising. As our economics team notes, "Chicago Fed President Goolsbee said rising energy prices and a potential oil shock pose stagflation risks – calling stagflation the worst-case scenario for central banks". Google Trends search data indicate an acceleration in searches for "stagflation" in recent weeks, driven by Singapore, Hong Kong and the US. Our energy team notes that with a one-month gas outage in Qatar (their base case), Asian buyers are likely to feel the pain sooner, and we also observe refinery run cuts and fuel conservation measures in that region, while the impact for Europe might come more slowly. Gold has historically performed well during periods of stagflation, as highlighted in Exhibit 5 which runs analysis from 1971 to 2021.

records.text: A New Direction Under a New Chair? With Jerome Powell’s term as chair ending in May, investors have begun to ask whether the Fed will take a new direction under President Trump’s nominee, Kevin Warsh. On interest rate policy, Warsh has been dovish in part because he has been confident that inflation is headed lower. While these views would position him on the dovish side of the FOMC’s recent debate, they would not represent a meaningful change from Chair Powell’s views. A potentially more significant change might be that a new chair is unlikely to immediately inherit the ability that Powell appeared to have to build a consensus at meetings where the data were not clear-cut and the FOMC was divided. On balance sheet policy, Warsh’s views have contrasted more strongly with those of other Fed officials. His specific proposal, to paraphrase it in the language of our financial conditions framework, is to substantially shrink the Fed’s balance sheet— putting duration back into the market and putting upward pressure on longer-term interest rates the way that a QT program would—in order to create room to simultaneously lower the funds rate, since the two actions would have offsetting effects on the overall stance of financial conditions. We think this is unlikely to happen, for a few reasons. Volume data from July 2020 onwards represents the combined total traded volume across EBS and Reuters sources. Prior to July 2020, we aggregate total traded volume from EBS with estimated trading volume from Reuters, which is calculated as a product of total paid-given count and average trade size. To estimate average trade size prior to July 2020 we use all future data for total trading volume and trade count. We then apply a 20-day moving average and rank the current value over the prior one-year lookback window**. In contrast, disruptions to global semiconductor production in 2022 affected trade worth around 1% of global GDP . More importantly, these products do not appear likely to create shortages in “critical” inputs that would lead to broad production shutdowns. Sulfur, nitrogen, and ammonia are used as fertilizers, which increases agricultural productivity but is not essential and could be rationed. Most limestone flux is produced domestically, and polyethylene is mostly used for production of low value add (and generally not essential) plastics. We therefore anticipate limited production challenges from these items. On the surface, helium would seem like the most likely candidate for potential supply disruptions given that is a hard-to-substitute input into production of MRI machines, semiconductors, and aerospace systems. But conversations with our equity analysts suggest that contracts for helium supply are generally long-term and fixed, and several large producers have enough helium stored to offset potential supply disruptions for the foreseeable future. However, over the last two months the tides have been shifting. The narrative moved from the assertion that AI-linked capex could buoy the economy to worries that AI-adoption could disrupt multiple industries , most notably software. The narrative of strong technicals has been challenged in recent weeks as record $IG supply along with increased cross-asset volatility and a potential shift in yield- buying activity has softened demand. The narrative of a resilient labor market that can maintain the low-fire/low-hire equilibrium, has given way to concerns that the labor market may be softening too much. And most recently, the narrative of fiscal benefits for consumers and businesses from the One Big Beautiful Bill is weakening as small business confidence wanes and higher energy prices absorb the consumer windfall. Since January, we have flagged a risk of the MAS reducing its policy accommodativeness in FX and rates this year, as Singapore goes through a reflationary phase (see Singapore: Reflation set to change MAS and market views, dated 7 January). Historically, this is usually done via an increase in the SGD NEER slope, which has a long-term average of 1.0% and is currently at 0.50%. Additionally, adjustments in FX policies have typically been accompanied by moves in SORA rates, as seen in the last two policy cycles (a tightening cycle in 2022 and a loosening cycle in 2025). The recent Middle East conflicts have added to inflation concerns, given Singapore's reliance on oil imports and limited reserves (see FX: Asia's sensitivity to supply- driven energy shocks, dated 10 March), increasing the likelihood of a hawkish move from the MAS in April. As Figure 16 below illustrates, 81% & 69% of B & CCC rated financing respectively across the entire spec-grade ecosystem is provided by the leveraged loan and private credit markets. And T+2 & T+3 maturity walls for B & CCC rated firms in the $HY & $Lev Loan market are still near all-time highs. In 2022-2023, rapid growth in private credit AUM helped liquefy lower-rated financing markets, at a time when the syndicated $HY bond & $Lev loan markets went dormant. But in 2026-2027, it is likely private credit fund outflows will do the reverse, leading to forced selling of $Lev Loans, and encouraging outflow risk from $HY, where we estimate 35% of the market is held by open-ended mutual funds & ETFs. We doubt a relative lack of software exposure will help $HY outright with that type of liquidity risk lurking in the background, again emanating from US retail. Who is more exposed? Within the region, EM Asia economies like the Philippines, Thailand, India and Indonesia will be more exposed to food price inflation risks (incidentally these are also the economies which are also exposed to fuel inflation risks). Given that central banks in these economies also target headline inflation, the potential rise in food inflation may be a concern to central banks and we highlight risks to the rate cuts we have in our base case for Indonesia and the Philippines. If the disruptions last for longer, we may get risks of rate hikes in India and the Philippines. In terms of output, India has the higher share of agriculture as 17% of GDP, followed by Indonesia at 13% and Thailand at 9%. We expect 2026 headline and core PCE inflation to be marked up to 2.8% and 2.7%, respectively, for two reasons: i) there have been substantial upside surprises in PCE inflation since the December meeting, and ii) oil prices have spiked due to the Iran war. While we see risks of core PCE coming in slightly below our expectations, if the Fed takes the Jan and Feb data on board, it will only take core PCE averaging 17bp through year-end for the 4q/4q rate to hit 2.7% (Exhibit 3). We expect no change in inflation in the out-years, but we wouldn’t be surprised if 2027 is also revised modestly higher. Growth for this year should also be marked up a tenth to 2.4%. This reflects i) underlying momentum in the economy, as 4Q/4Q 2025 growth came in well above the Fed’s Dec projection of 1.7%, and ii) payback for a larger-than-expected drag from the 4Q 2025 government shutdown. That said, policymakers might decide to leave their 2026 growth forecasts unchanged, given the potential downside risks from oil. We don't see a compelling case for growth to get revised higher in the out-years. But we do see room for longer-run growth to get marked up, given that GDP has substantially outpaced the Fed's longer-run estimate (1.8%) in the last three years. A markup to longer-run growth could also lift the 2027-28 growth forecasts on the margin.

Because the impact of flows on future returns also depends on the positions of institutions in that currency, the FXHRI is, with the FXHI, designed to quantify and measure empirically this aspect of investor behaviour. The indicator is updated on a daily basis with a two -day publication lag. We publish foreign currency hedge ratios against multi-asset portfolios and are able to disaggregate this multi -asset hedge ratio into hedges against equity assets and fixed income assets. FX Behavioural Factor Flows and Factor Holdings measure real-money demand for and positioning in FX factors. At a high level, the indicators reveal whether real -money investors are leaning into or leaning out of a given FX factor (e.g. carry, value, momentum). The indicators aggregate single currency indicators, including the Foreign Exchange Flow Indicator (FXFI) and Foreign Exchange Holdings Indicator (FXHI), into broader factor aggregates. The indicators cover seven regions: Global, Global ex-pegs, Global ex-USD, G10, G10 ex- USD, Emerging Markets, and Emerging Markets ex-pegs. Hauser highlighted the upside risks to inflation through local fuel prices. At current FX-ad- justed levels of Brent crude, we think this channel will deliver an additional 0.7%-pt upside to near-term inflation. However, he also flagged the GDP drag that may accompany the supply shock, while also calling out the disinflationary mix of the 4Q GDP data, productivity lift and better news on unit labour costs. Next week’s RBA meeting is a close call and developments in the Middle East, alongside the path of oil prices in coming days, will likely prove decisive for the outcome. Notably, net issuance of medium- to long-term loans (mostly mortgages) to households moderated to only RMB165bn in the first two months of this year, compared with RMB379bn in the same period last year, corresponding to the sluggish housing market momentum .
