Food prices are 5.4%Y, with restaurant prices at 7.8%Y and grocery inflation at 4.1%. The moderation in grocery inflation was broad-based, with one of the largest contributions coming from slower growth in fresh or frozen beef prices, which rose 13.9%Y compared with 18.8%Y in January. The GST/HST holiday also created visible base effects in food services. Restaurant prices were directly affected by the tax exemption, and as those artificially low prices fall out of the 12-month comparison window they continue to distort the annual inflation profile. Although grocery inflation is easing at the margin, price levels remain substantially higher than before the recent inflation surge, with grocery prices now 30.1% higher than in February 2021. Energy prices continue to provide a significant offset to food-driven inflation pressures. Gasoline prices declined 14.2% year over year in February, while natural gas prices fell 17.1%, exerting meaningful downward pressure on headline inflation. However, in coming months, dual headwinds are likely to raise energy inflation- first, the effects of the carbon tax removal on April 1, 2025 are going to fade beginning with the April print. In the first, we create a similarity score for a candidate’s profile relative to the professional attributes of prior holders of each ECB Executive Board role. In the second we introduce more nuanced criteria related to political bargaining and use these to ‘penalise’ the similarity score. Layer one – similarity score: We quantify the CVs of former and current EB members to define typical profiles. In addition to nationality and age, we record their years of experience in central banks, other European and international institutions, ministries, treasuries, academia, and the private sector. We note tenure in senior positions and board memberships, as well as whether the candidate holds a PhD or a professorial chair. We use a dimensional-reduction technique to project these variables onto two dimensions to visualise the data, then apply the same transformation for the candidates, to position their data in the same space. Using this two-dimensional representation, we identify the typical regions for each EB role based on historical and current EB members and compute the distance from each candidate to these clusters (Figure 8). Differences in investor constraints help explain why IG, HY, and Loans can sometimes demonstrate varying trajectories on the same underlying signal. Balance sheet anchored markets like IG will have more price stability compared with flow-driven markets like HY that remain highly sensitive to sentiment, liquidity, and flows Similarly, within the Loan market, CLOs suppress day-to-day volatility through structurally mandated demand, but also lead to concentration of risk. Manufacturing investment also improved and rose 3.1%, while real estate investment contracted further, to a lesser rate of 11.1%. A return to stronger growth in both infrastructure and manufacturing investment could reflect the government’s growing focus on jumpstarting growth through “effective” investment while maintaining its determination to rebalance the economy by reducing the economy’s reliance on housing investment. In particular, innovation-driven growth and the development of new quality productivity has remained a priority, and investment in high-tech industries increased 5.1%oya in January-February, 3.3pts higher than total investment, with high-tech manufacturing and services investment rising 2.9% and 10.0%, respectively. Investment in aviation, spacecraft and equipment manufacturing increased 20.2%, and investment in R&D and design services increased 20.6%. Another key aspect of rebalancing is boosting consumption. Retail sales growth rose to 0.6%m/m sa, or 2.8%oya (vs. JPMf: 2.1%oya, consensus: 2.5%) in January- February, from 0.2%m/m sa in December. This is the typical flow pattern for geopolitical conflicts which drive a VIX spike, wider credit spreads and equity market corrections. Geographically: The equity markets of countries (Canada, Brazil, Norway, US) that are net exporters of oil/natural gas and not as impacted by the Strait of Hormuz closing in addition to energy, defense and metals/mining sector funds are outperforming versus net importers/consumer. On a manager basis, we monitored positive/improving net flow results from AB, Amundi, BLK, CNS, DWS, FHI, IVZ, JHG, Jupiter, LAZ, MS, PIMCO, PRU, SCHW, Schroders, Vanguard and WT due mainly to their FI, passive equity/ETF and MMF businesses. Given our LT industry thesis (reallocations into ETFs/fixed income/Alts) and NT thesis of “flight to safety”, we rate BLK at Buy which has outperformed in other volatile periods. We also rate AMG at a Buy (AQR first-mover tax aware advantage) while AMG’s net flow trajectory could be impacted by the market correction. Update on key secular / cyclical themes: Re-risking & duration extensions (cyclical) – mixed: Active equity strengthened, while passive equity held steady. records.text: The most important developments since the last FOMC meeting are the start of n the war in Iran and the spike in oil prices. We recently raised our December 2026 year-over-year headline PCE inflation forecast by 0.8pp to 2.9% and our core PCE forecast by 0.2pp to 2.4%, lowered our 2026 Q4/Q4 GDP growth forecast by 0.3pp to 2.2%, and raised our peak unemployment rate forecast by 0.1pp to 4.6%. For the Fed, the war increases both the risk that earlier rate cuts will be needed to address labor market softening and the risk that a higher inflation path will delay cuts. Against this backdrop, the FOMC is set to leave the funds rate unchanged at n 3.5-3.75% this week and is likely to note in its statement that the war has increased uncertainty about the outlook and will likely raise inflation and weigh on economic activity in the near term. We expect three dissents in favor of a 25bp cut, with Governor Bowman now joining Governors Miran and Waller. The Summary of Economic Projections is likely to show changes to the 2026 n forecasts similar to our own, including higher core (+0.2pp to 2.7% Q4/Q4) and headline (+0.6pp to 3.0%) inflation, lower GDP growth (-0.2pp to 2.1%), and a higher unemployment rate (+0.2pp to 4.6%). We expect little change on net in the dots, where the median is likely to continue to show one cut in each of 2026 and 2027. records.text: M Idea 2 Deja Vu? As discussed in last week’s note, we believe the current equity market correction began last fall when liquidity started to tighten. As soon as funding markets started to show stress from that tightening, the Fed responded by announcing it would end its balance sheet reduction program (QT) earlier than expected. It followed that up by restarting asset purchases in December. This pivot subsequently led to the better equity performance in January, in our view. It also happened alongside a sharp decline in the US dollar and concentrated returns in emerging markets and commodity-oriented sectors like gold/silver, industrial metals, oil and memory stocks. More recently, the dollar has rallied and these same areas have noticeably cooled off. More on the dollar later. Before the events in Iran 2 weeks ago, the correction was very well advanced in both time and price, with many stocks down 20%, or more. In fact, 50% of all stocks in the Russell 3000 are now down 20% from their 52-week highs. For the S&P 500, this number is over 40%. records.text: M Idea Morgan Stanley Research 5 The third offset is the IEA-coordinated strategic stock release. At first glance, the headline number is impressive: member countries have announced a collective release of 400 million barrels, the largest in the IEA’s history. But the relevant constraint is flow rate, not stock volume. Historically, the highest release rate from the collective strategic reserves of IEA members was around 1.3 mb/d in late 2022. Given the severity of the current disruption, the system may be pushed harder this time, but a sustained release rate much above 2 mb/d would still be surprising. There is also a regional mismatch. A large share of the release comes from the United States, while much of the prompt crude shortage is in Asia, and the voyage from the US Gulf Coast to India is around 30 days under normal conditions. Put differently, barrels in storage are not the same thing as barrels arriving in Asia on time. Strategic stocks therefore help to cushion the blow and may stabilise sentiment, but they do not solve the immediate physical shortage where it is most acute. When a major disruption in crude and products starts to push up the price of fueling ships in key Asian ports, the shock is no longer confined to upstream supply losses. It is beginning to spill over into the logistics system itself. These dislocations matter because product shortages are even harder to solve than crude shortages. Strategic crude stocks can cushion headline balances, but they do not directly replace missing jet fuel into Europe, naphtha into Asian petrochemical plants or bunker supply in major ports. Refineries need time to adjust, substitute crudes do not produce identical product yields, and trade flows need time to re-optimize. That is why cracks and regional shortages may remain severe even if some crude supply is restored. In practical terms, the market may have to ration demand in products well before the crude balance looks fully resolved. Given these offsetting considerations, we expect the Governing Council will maintain its assessment that policy is “in about the right place” and leave its guidance broadly unchanged. records.text: Warsh has also argued that the Fed should substantially shrink its balance sheet, n allowing it to lower the funds rate to offset the impact on financial conditions. We think this is unlikely to happen, for a few reasons. First, we do not think there is substantial room to shrink the balance sheet without abandoning the ample reserves framework, which has broad support within the Federal Reserve. Second, if the Treasury thinks about the consolidated government balance sheet and accounts for the equilibrium size of the Fed’s balance sheet in its issuance decisions, then changing the size of the Fed’s balance sheet should not have an impact on the debt available to the public and therefore on interest rates. Third, even if the Fed could substantially shrink its balance sheet and the Treasury did not adapt its debt issuance in response, we are doubtful that lowering short-run interest rates at the expense of raising long-run rates would be popular. 15 March 2026 2 Goldman Sachs US Economics Analyst For the exclusive use of CAYLA.BUETTNER@BLUECRESTCAPITAL.COM 7595159db82544668b3260609400172c

records.text: 6 Liquid Insight | 16 March 2026 USD: bigger forces at play Wednesday’s FOMC is unlikely to be a pivotal event for the USD in this environment. No expected policy changes are on the horizon, and geopolitically-driven uncertainty is rising by the day, keeping the USD supported. The overall messaging and tone from Chair Powell will likely underscore these increased uncertainties, while any revealed bias on the inflation or growth risks will likely be quickly digested by the FX market. For now, the USD market should remain primarily headline-driven, with oil markets setting the pace. As long as current events keep upward pressure on oil, USD upside risks will remain, particularly against those currencies more vulnerable to a terms-of-trade shock (EUR, GBP, JPY, SEK, NZD, CHF). Any USD upside vs those more insulated (AUD, CAD, NOK) will be driven by overall market risk sentiment. For now, the USD’s move against most G10 currencies has been mitigated at the margin by broader central bank repricing. Indeed, the move higher in rates has been global, and the Fed is now the only G10 central bank not priced for some odds of a hike this year. Any further pricing out of these Fed cuts, particularly amid elevated global growth concerns, should continue to support the USD.

For both, current 5 -day flows are in the 5 th percentile, indicating that selling shows little sign of abating. At the other end of the spectrum, the AUD is the only currency (apart from the USD) where 20-day flows are now stronger than they were before the start of the conflict. Albeit, AUD 20 -day flows then were in just the 28th percentile and they are in the 38th now. The latest week of flow data (up and to including Wednesday) has also seen renewed (presumably safe-haven inspired) buying of the CHF. CHF 5 -day flows are in the 65 th percentile (seco nd only to the USD in 5-day ranking). Figure 7 US Treasury flows Still selling Treasuries Even though we are seeing renewed and strong buying of the USD this has not translated into real money buying of US Treasuries. 20 -day day flows to UST nominals has picked up a little since the conflict started (albeit from the zero percentile to the 16th ) but remain weak overall. Arguably more surprisingly, given the market fears over the inflationary impact of higher oil prices and subsequent sharp increase in rate expectations across the G10 , we are not seeing any pick-up in buying of US TIPS. 20-day TIPS flows have actually fallen to the zero percentile, down from the 28 th percentile on February 27 th. Even at current levels, the dollar value of oil consumption as a share of global GDP is already moving back toward ranges that have historically started to weigh on growth, though still below the peaks reached in the late 1970s and early 2010s. If the market is forced into rationing, prices may therefore not rise smoothly through every intermediate level. They may instead move relatively quickly toward the zone where enough demand is actually destroyed. In practical terms, that suggests a prolonged Hormuz closure would require prices in the order of $130-150/bbl to rebalance the market. This episode is a powerful reminder that stocks matter, which points to higher desired precautionary inventories in more countries and therefore a somewhat firmer floor under crude demand. M Idea Morgan Stanley Research 3 Supply Disruption Risks – A Focus on Food Rising risks of supply disruption as conflict persists: As geopolitical tensions persist, the challenges for the region will build up. In last Wednesday’s report (The Viewpoint: Tracking Disruption Risks Across Asia, 11 Mar 2026), we had explained the potential supply chain disruptions on account of the energy price shock and potential cuts in quantities of oil, gas, fertilizers, petrochemicals and other commodities where exports from the Middle East (ME) account for a much larger share. Turning our focus to food: In this report, we highlight the transmission channels of higher energy and related commodity prices through to food. Just like oil, Asia is relatively more exposed to food inflation considering that food’s share in the consumption basket is much larger than in the US and Europe. Indeed, food accounts for about 25% of Asia’s CPI basket as compared to 13% for the US and 14% for the Euro Area. Rise in global food prices has been less pronounced than fuel so far: So far global food prices have risen by just about 6% since Feb 26, as compared to the more than 40% rise in international oil and fertilizer (ME urea) prices. However, if the Iran conflict continues, food prices could rise with a lag and so we are watching for potential upside risks to inflation from this channel. records.text: The BoC is set to remain on hold this week, with both consensus forecasters (25 out of 25 forecasters expect a hold) and market pricing (-2bp) placing little odds on a policy rate change. We expect that the statement will acknowledge the softer spot data but note that headline inflation will increase due to higher oil prices. Given these offsetting considerations, we expect the Governing Council will maintain its assessment that policy is “in about the right place” and leave its guidance broadly unchanged. The main hawkish risk is that the Governing Council upgrades their assessment of the balance of risks given the coming boosts to growth and inflation from oil price increases, but we view a hawkish pivot as highly unlikely given softer spot data and uncertainty around the upcoming USMCA negotiations. Supply resilience continued with industrial production (IP) beating at 6.3%YoY (Citi/Mkt: 5.0%YoY, Prior: 5.2%YoY). The demand side remained lackluster but defied subdued market expectations, with retail sales up 2.8%YoY (Citi/Mkt: 3.0/2.1%YoY, Prior: 0.9%YoY) and fixed asset investment 1.8%YoY (Citi/Mkt: 1.5/-4.2%YoY, Prior: -3.8%YoY Ytd) – both above expectations. The familiar pattern persisted: supply outpacing demand, new economy outperforming old economy. However, the headline beats don’t alleviate our concerns around the K-shaped recovery. Risks to our 26Q1E growth forecasts are tilted towards the upside, with nominal GDP poised for a stronger rebound than real growth. We are aware of some one- off factors behind this: Stronger-than-expected exports supported IP partially due to the favorable calendar effect, and we cannot rule out some payback in March. The small beat in retail sales came from the holiday economy, and reduced trade-in subsidies this year may weigh on growth. The rebound in FAI was almost fully driven by infrastructure investment. Smaller Fed sheet could be through TT&L return Proposals to accelerate Fed balance-sheet reduction have resurfaced alongside renewed debate over the appropriate size/mix of Fed liabilities. The Fed’s main liabilities are (1) currency (2) TGA (3) reserve balances. This note focuses on how TGA, capping or actively managing it, could help deliver a smaller Fed balance sheet (similar to pre-GFC). We also compare this to Canada’s RG auctions and UK DMO’s cash management. TGA minimum = ~$825b and rising The Treasury’s cash balance is a liability on the Fed’s balance sheet that is largely out of the Fed’s control. The Treasury aims to hold, at a minimum, the sum of expected outflows over the next 5-days. YTD, 5-day outflows have averaged around $825bn but see shifts higher around large paydowns or tax refund season. Flows into the TGA typically come out of reserves which can create volatility in reserves around UST settlement and tax dates. In theory, the Fed can limit or cap the total funds held in TGA. From 28 January when the AI disruption trade started roiling markets €IG and €HY spreads are 18bps and 53bps wider respectively, not even half of their widening around Liberation Day and coming from very compressed levels. However, with cash spreads accelerating their widening over the last couple of sessions, cash spread resilience has come into question and in combination with the sell-off in rates has taken ytd total returns decisively negative across the board though (Figure 20). But between €IG & €HY, we believe two different stories have been playing out in the background that should also impact future returns. While €IG has yet to show major outflows and continued to see inflows in all of February despite AI-disruption and private credit concerns roiling markets, €HY has already seen more than half of its ytd inflows reverse within a span of two weeks (Figure 21). And inflows had already stalled before tensions in the Middle East escalated, underpinning that AI- disruption and private credit concerns that we think will disproportionately affect spec-grade issuers (also see IG Winners, HY Losers? ), have also seen investors exercise more caution. The market has moved from expecting more than two Fed cuts this year to pricing fewer than one, this along with the sell-off in bonds and equities is tightening financial conditions. Our economists now expect the first cut in September (rather than June), followed by a second in December, reaching a terminal rate of 3.0-3.25%. The longer oil stays elevated, the greater the risk that inflation spillovers weaken the bond market and trigger an equity de-rating at the index level and of course in turn tighter FCIs (Exhibit 6). In addition, labour market data are losing momentum (see the February payrolls), arguably reducing the economy’s resilience to further shocks. Although on the flip side this may also prevent the pass-through of energy cost inflation into core and allow for easier policy. 6. AI disruption concerns and rotation beneath the surface already signal vulnerability. Investors are increasingly questioning the sustainability of capital-light business models, the rotation from Software and Intangibles toward physical infrastructure—trends that were already underway before the conflict. At the same time, anecdotal evidence points to early signs of credit stress – especially in private areas, which are still small but have grown the most - consistent with tighter financial conditions, even if not yet systemic. While some regional economies are highly exposed—our Middle Eastern economics team sees significant headwinds to regional growth—non-energy exports account for less than 1% of total imports for major DMs and EMs, and only 1% of total global trade. Where risk is absorbed – and stored Alt managers’ growing footprint has implications for both stability and risk transmission in credit. Limited mark-to-market and flexible capital structure offerings have helped cushion volatility and suppress public default rates, but increasing scale, low transparency, and liquidity mismatch can also store risk and transmit stress when conditions tighten. Stress travels through owners, not instruments Spillovers from one asset class to another only become clear through an ownership lens. Permanent capital can absorb shocks, but it can also extend mispricing and allow dislocation to persist. Investors should factor in the marginal holder of each asset class and map transmission channels across owners to get a holistic credit market picture. records.text: 16 March 2026 IG & HY Strategy Page 20 Deutsche Bank AG €-Credit: Put to the Test After credit spreads started the year not far off their all-time lows and €IG spreads even advanced to new ones, the market backdrop has become more challenging. First, fears about AI disruption, private credit and ever expanding hyperscaler capex started to roil markets at the end of January and then the war in Iran and an energy price shock added another headwind that will likely reverberate in coming months. This has already put to the test what has been an extremely resilient market in €IG and €HY thanks to extraordinarily strong technicals. That said, even before the escalation of tensions in the Middle East, cracks had started to appear in the €-Credit space, starting from the lowest end of the rating spectrum. With weakness from the € leveraged loan market finding its way into B-rated bonds, €HY has no longer been able to keep pace with €IG since last Fall and we have seen €HY underperform in the first phase of the AI-disruption driven sell-off in late January/early February also in relative terms (Figure 19). Since then other drivers have taken over the spread trajectory temporarily but we expect the pattern to keep resurfacing. records.text: M Idea 6 Housing a Slowdown Housing faces policy pressure: The housing market has been strong over the past 12 months, but the hawkish shift from the RBA has already started to spur softening, with housing sentiment measures having fallen over the past few months, auction clearance rates lower, and sequential price increases slowing. Further rate hikes will add more pressure. On top of this, the government is mulling several housing-related tax increases including changes to the capital gains tax discount and negative gearing. Citi's Most Read – Economics March 9 - March 15 Most Read Most Read US Economics - CPI inflation slowing more than PCE February core CPI rose 0.216%MoM, closely in line with our and consensus expectations. Shelter inflation continues to slow and should remain softer than usual on average throughout this year as home prices and rents have been soft for some time. Services prices slowed after start-of-year strength in January. Core goods prices rose modestly, with tariff pass-through for certain components likely to fade in coming months. But February data feels somewhat stale in the context of new upside risks for inflation and core goods prices, such as higher energy costs. And despite softer core goods in CPI for a few months, differences in weights in PCE inflation will mean much stronger core goods prices already in PCE inflation. With CPI data, we are tracking 0.42%MoM core PCE inflation in February (which will change next week). This should keep Fed officials cautious on inflation risks and on hold for now. records.text: M Update 2 February CPI: Cooling, for now Bank of Canada Implications This print was in line with the Bank of Canada's forecasts for a temporary undershoot in headline inflation, before a convergence to target. We expect the Bank to remain on hold this week, and for the rest of this year. We continue to expect the Bank's next move to be a hike in 1Q2027. We see two-sided risks to our call: after the Friday labor market report, we think that the BoC will continue to assess any exaggerated weakness in the activity data relative to its baseline which account for structural changes. Our oil strategists meanwhile see oil prices remaining elevated through 2Q and 3Q. With a more persistent shock to oil, we see symmetric risks around the BoC's next move. • For the second successive month, CPI-Trim and CPI-Median remain below 2.5% on a 12-month basis and 1.5% on a 3-month annualized basis. Given the current market narrative is starting to turn upside down, we make some surprising calls below. n First, prefer long-duration rates over credit. This isn’t early 2022 pre- Russia/Ukraine, where central bank policy was massively stimulative. Today, real central bank policy rates are restrictive and labour markets are struggling, hurting consumer confidence. We doubt rate hikes being priced in Europe & the UK will be realized. But a longer hold from the Fed/ECB/BOE through the first half of this year will still act to slow growth and tighten financial conditions, forcing a flattening of rate curves, and then eventually, lower long-duration yields. n Second, cash credit should underperform synthetics tactically. Cash spreads in all markets trade expensive to synthetics (Fig 9), as higher rates encourage yield buyers to buy bonds, while issuances temporarily slows. But this setup isn’t sustainable. If the Iran conflict forces higher commodity prices for longer, higher rates will damage total returns, leading to fund outflows, and will eventually force down long-end sovereign yields as growth weakens. If the current conflict ends sooner than expected, lower sovereign yields and pent-up corporate issuance will lead to cash underperformance. n Third, position for more HY/IG decompression, particularly in the 1H’26. records.text: 16 March 2026 IG & HY Strategy Deutsche Bank AG Page 5 European Summary: Thanks to AI disruption fears, private credit concerns, geopolitical tensions and an energy price shock, the market backdrop has become more challenging and we expect spreads to widen moderately from current levels. But particularly in €IG resilient technicals should limit the widening and keep spreads from trading far off current levels for long. The primary theme will be one of more decompression and dispersion, most notably between the IG and HY markets with spec-grade issuers more vulnerable to the mix of new headwinds. We favor €IG over €HY and see €HY at risk of continued outflows. Within €IG, we prefer A and better rated bonds for now but recommend to use (so far absent) decompression in BBBs to increase exposure as we expect yield buying to eventually provide support. Conversely, we advise more caution on BB rated bonds. The latter are likely to face more scrutiny and could be used to raise liquidity in HY- portfolios, meaning further €HY spread widening should not be confined to Bs. We prefer hybrids, Bank Tier-2 debt and Insurance subs to HY-Seniors Sector positioning should also be key as dispersion rises from very low levels. Andrew Hollenhorst | Veronica Clark | Gisela Young Market pricing around 40bp in cuts this year Australia Economics - RBA to front-load the hiking cycle; 25bps hike in March and May to a terminal of 4.35% The economy is operating under a positive output gap. Meanwhile, an oil shock could linger longer than expected and threaten to raise inflation. We revise our inflation forecasts for 2026, with headline inflation at 4.1% and trimmed-mean inflation at 3.7% by mid-year. Add to this a strong labour market and the hawkish rhetoric from Deputy Governor Hauser suggests that the RBA staff want to act quicker rather than later to curb inflationary pressures. Thus the front-loaded hiking cycle we mentioned at the start of the year now looks more plausible. Consequently, we change our view and now see the RBA hiking by 25bps across March and May for a terminal rate of 4.35%. We expect the Bank keep policy rates restrictive across H226 as higher oil prices filter through the economy, with rate cuts still expected in 2027. records.text: 1. The rise in oil prices is worsening the growth/inflation mix while ERPs are low. Brent crude around $100 reflects the sharp increase in geopolitical risk, and our commodity analysts now assume 21 days of reduced flows through the Strait of Hormuz (vs. 10 previously). Their central scenario sees Brent averaging $98 in March– April—around 40% above the 2025 average—before falling back to $71 by 4Q26, while an extreme scenario could see prices reach $150 and remain elevated. Even the central case slows US GDP by 0.3pp to 2.2% and our US economists have raised their recession probability to 25% (from 20%); in Europe, where impacts are nonlinear under prolonged disruption, recession risks are significantly higher. Higher oil prices also increase the risk of inflation spillovers weakening the bond market; this is especially worrisome for equities when ERPs have already fallen and are back to pre-GFC levels (Exhibit 1). 2. Such large moves can erode multiple days of carry in short-gamma positions, especially if the positions were initiated when implieds were at historically low levels. As we have noted previously, the first few weeks of the year created a favorable backdrop for carry-seeking short-gamma strategies because yields were mostly rangebound. However, the Iran conflict has introduced elevated jump risk into markets (Interest Rate Derivatives, US Fixed Income Markets Weekly, 3/6/2026), which is a risk to short-gamma positions due to the nonlinear nature of gamma returns. Indeed, markets did not deliver enough volatility in January and February to overcome theta decay, but they have in the past two weeks in shorter tails (Fig- ure 12 ). Therefore, yesterday's large daily move likely was likely exacerbated by unwinds of carry-seeking short-gamma positions. records.text: M Idea Morgan Stanley Research 3 markets have been worried about AI disruption/labor impacts, private credit defaults and liquidity tightness well before the Iran conflict escalated. Interestingly but not surprisingly, crude and the Vix did begin their rise in January, signaling the market was ahead of this risk, too. Corrections typically don’t end until the best stocks and highest quality indices get hit, and that usually takes a capitulatory shock. Last year, this was Liberation Day; this time around, that event is the Iran conflict and concern about a sustained rise in crude prices above $100/bbl. This final corrective phase has begun, in our view, with the S&P 500 having its worst two-week stretch since last April. As a result of the "mini capitulation" and spike in volatility last Monday, some hedges were removed or monetized, though index downside still remains well hedged at this point. The equity market appears to be discounting a resolution to the conflict, and a reopening of the Strait of Hormuz in weeks, not months. Should that perception change due to an additional surprise, equity markets would likely experience broader capitulation than what we saw last Monday, but that could also mark the final/durable low like last year’s Liberation Day, albeit with less downside. records.text: Paths to Further Rate Cuts We recently pushed the two additional rate cuts in our forecast back to September and December. By September, we expect that both moderate further labor market softening and progress on underlying inflation—admittedly an increasingly murky concept with both tariffs and now higher energy costs passing through to the core—will contribute to the case for a cut. If instead the labor market weakens sooner and more substantially than we expect, we do not think that concern about the impact of higher oil prices on inflation and inflation expectations would be an obstacle to earlier rate cuts. We continue to see the risks over the next year as tilted to the downside of our 3-3.25% terminal rate forecast. The FOMC could choose a slightly lower terminal rate if inflation falls to or below 2% next year, it could deliver another package of insurance cuts if a new risk arises, and it would likely cut substantially if a recession occurred. Reflecting these possibilities, our probability-weighted Fed forecast remains more dovish than both our baseline forecast and market pricing (Exhibit 7). Turning our focus to food: In this report, we highlight the transmission channels of higher energy and related commodity prices through to food. Just like oil, Asia is relatively more exposed to food inflation considering that food’s share in the consumption basket is much larger than in the US and Europe. Indeed, food accounts for about 25% of Asia’s CPI basket as compared to 13% for the US and 14% for the Euro Area. The rise in global food prices has been less pronounced than fuel so far: So far global food prices have risen by just about 6% since Feb 26, as compared to the more than 40% rise in international oil and fertilizer (ME urea) prices. However, if the Iran conflict continues, food prices could rise with a lag and so we are watching for potential upside risks to inflation from this channel. As it is, the production cost structure for food is also linked to fuel (for powering farm equipment) and fertilisers, with the other costs being labour, seed and irrigation. Key inputs like fertilizer and fuel will eventually pass through. Although the processes clearly differ, the allocation of top European posts – including at the ECB – shares features with the papal succession, functioning as a set of bargaining games where candidates must show sufficient prestige, credibility and consensus-building ability to progress. We therefore think the Bocconi framework’s philosophy resonates well with the succession at the ECB. Model candidates: With Bocconi’s analysis as inspiration, we develop a quantitative assignment method that accounts for top-level reshuffles and measures each candidate’s proximity to their predecessors. The model evaluates professional suitability (i.e. career path, sector experience) and incorporates member-state power distribution and outcome complexity for the high number of rotating positions. By layering inputs to capture each critical dimension, we hope to answer the central question of who is ‘papabile’ in a structured, data-driven manner. records.text: arnings What Is Driving the Need to Hike? The RBA is not well placed to look through a supply shock. Inflation was already above target and had risen further over the past six months, which was the key catalyst for the RBA to shift back to tightening at the February meeting. The RBA is clearly uncomfortable with the path that inflation is likely to take over the next few months (we estimate that a US$100/bbl oil price would push headline inflation up ~70bps, against an RBA June 2026 forecast that was already 4.2%Y). We think it wants to be seen as acting against this to try and contain inflation expectations. The corollary of this is that there appears to be a greater acceptance and willingness to see growth slow as a consequence, particularly given the still wide uncertainty around the depth and breadth of the growth consequences of this current oil shock. The RBA appears willing to accept this, prioritising a view of moving inflation back to target faster.

Northern coalition: The Netherlands, Austria, Finland and the Baltic states are typically associated with a stronger inflation-credibility bias. Klaas Knot, Dutch central bank president until last year, is widely cited as a leading contender. While no longer a sitting governor, he would provide continuity and over time has evolved to become a more centrist and pragmatic policymaker, particularly in navigating post-pandemic tightening and the subsequent easing cycle. We think this shift may broaden his appeal beyond the traditional hawkish bloc, strengthening his potential candidacy as a more consensual figure in a qualified-majority-vote scenario. Eastern member states: These member states have gained weight in the eurozone arithmetic. But with Croatian Governor Boris Vujčić appointed vice-president only recently, there is little pressure for further representation. Beyond the presidency: If political constraints prevent Germany or France from securing the presidency, they might prioritise securing another operationally critical seat instead. records.text: ab 16 March 2026 Global Research Asia FI/FX Strategy Oil Up, Hikes priced - Will Central Banks Act? Asia’s Oil Disruption: Markets pricing Hikes - Will Central Banks Act? Oil disruptions have pushed front-end oil futures 50% above central banks' assumptions. Our simulations—assuming a 10% oil rise lifts average EM Asia CPI by ~25bp—suggest that even if oil prices average around 85$/bbl (same as 6m futures), select central banks' inflation targets could be breached, most clearly in PH, KR and ID. Markets are as such pricing aggressive rate hikes: four hikes each in Korea and India over the next two years, and six in Taiwan. Will policy validate this? The bar for broad-based tightening is high. Growth risks are underpriced, and so is the likelihood that fiscal policy —not monetary—does the heavy lifting in a stagflationary shock. As argued in Oil Shock Aftermath: Uneven Risk Pricing, value is re-emerging in front-end rates. Why we think the bar for Rate hikes Is High If oil averages US$80+ in H2, calibrated hikes may seem intuitive—but the bar is high for five reasons. First, unprecedented supply shock (>10% of global oil supply) raises energy rationing risks while hurting domestic demand. Historical sensitivities suggest oil at $80– 90/bbl could shave ~60bp off EM Asia GDP , or send EM Asia ex TW growth to be 1ppt below trend; PH and TH most exposed, MY least. records.text: The March Meeting The FOMC statement is likely to acknowledge that the war has increased uncertainty about the outlook and is likely to raise inflation and weigh on economic activity in the near term (Exhibit 4). In light of the downward revision last week to 2025Q4 GDP growth, the statement will also likely describe activity growth as “moderate” rather than “solid.” And in light of the latest employment news, the Committee will likely modestly downgrade its description of the labor market. We expect three dissents in favor of a 25bp cut because we suspect that the latest labor market data will push Governor Bowman to join Governors Miran and Waller, who had also dissented in January. The Summary of Economic Projections is likely to show changes to the 2026 forecasts similar to our own, including higher core (+0.2pp to 2.7% Q4/Q4) and headline (+0.6pp to 3.0% Q4/Q4) inflation, lower GDP growth (-0.2pp to 2.1% Q4/Q4), and a higher unemployment rate (+0.2pp to 4.6% in Q4). These changes to the economic projections would have roughly offsetting implications for the funds rate. Supply update Last month, the CBO released an update of its 10-year budget projections, incorporating changes deriving from tariffs, immigration actions, and the OBBBA. Following the release, we have updated our own deficit projections, although differences remain between CBO’s projections and our own. Notably, CBO published these estimates prior to the Supreme Court ruling on IEEPA. The administration has replaced IEEPA with a 10% tariff under Section 122, which we estimate brings the observed average US effective tariff rate from 9.4% to 7.6% (see Winners and losers of the tariff reshuffle, 2/27/26). New investigations have also been opened under Sections 301 and 232, which we expect to eventually push the tariff rate back towards IEEPA levels. We estimate that IEEPA accounted for roughly $150- 200bn of the tariff revenue collected thus far, and we assume 60-70% of that will be refunded in FY27. Net of all factors, we now expect a deficit of $1.875tn in FY2026, and a deficit of $2.0tn in FY2027, versus our previous forecast of $1.955tn and $2.047tn, respectively.
